title: Manufacturing
note: Processes remove material (machining), shape it (casting, forging, molding, extrusion), join it (welding, fastening), or add it layer by layer (3D printing). Tolerances state how far a dimension may vary while the part still works; tighter tolerances cost more.

read.title: Choosing how to make it
text: A design is not finished until someone can make it. Manufacturing processes fall into a few families. Subtractive processes such as turning, milling, and drilling cut material away from solid stock; a CNC machine runs them from a digital program. Forming processes shape material without removing it: casting pours liquid metal into a mold, forging hammers or presses hot metal, extrusion pushes it through a die, and injection molding forces molten plastic into a steel mold.

Choice depends on volume, material, and geometry. Injection molding needs an expensive mold but makes each extra part for pennies, so it suits millions of identical parts. Machining needs no special tooling, so it suits a handful.

Additive manufacturing builds parts layer by layer. FDM extrudes plastic filament and is cheap but leaves visible layers and weaker bonds between them. SLA cures liquid resin with ultraviolet light for fine detail. SLS fuses nylon powder with a laser, and the loose powder supports overhangs.
Whatever the process, no part comes out exactly to size. Engineers specify tolerances so parts still fit and work, and they loosen tolerances wherever they can, because precision costs money.

q.q: Why does injection molding suit very high volumes?
o: The mold is expensive but each extra part is cheap
It needs no tooling at all

q.q: Which process supports overhangs with loose powder?
Why do engineers loosen tolerances where they can?
o: Tolerances are required to be loose by law
